title: Dog-Trade Defenses Need Evidence, Not Tradition Claims
excerpt: Rabies can kill after symptoms begin. Pet theft and uninspected transport demand proof, traceability, and reform—not tradition claims without records.
body_html:
A rabies exposure can become fatal when care comes too late. WHO states that rabies is virtually 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear. Immediate wound washing and urgent medical assessment matter. This health risk stands beside, not as proof of, any single commercial supply chain. It shows why every animal movement, slaughter site, and inspection record must face scrutiny.

Tradition cannot erase missing records

“Tradition” does not prove humane sourcing, lawful transport, veterinary inspection, or food safety. “Farm-raised dogs” does not prove origin either. A credible claim needs traceable breeding records, ownership records, vaccination history, transport documents, quarantine compliance, and inspection evidence. Without those records, buyers and communities cannot distinguish lawful activity from stolen pets or illegally moved animals.

Pet theft causes direct family harm. Criminal operators who steal companion animals turn trust into profit. Claims about stolen-dog networks require case-specific police records, court judgments, or seizure reports. Those records should be published and investigated. No family should carry burden of proving where its missing dog went while traders face no traceability duty.

Biosecurity starts before exposure

Rabies usually spreads when infected saliva enters through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and bite attacks create separate risks. After possible exposure, wash wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes. Seek urgent medical care for post-exposure prophylaxis, including vaccine and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Treatment must begin before symptoms develop.

Vietnamese families, veterinarians, local officials, and animal-protection leaders can close these gaps. Public health targets and enforcement measures are not the same as SDE’s campaign demand: complete abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition calling for nationwide abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition and add your name to a public demand for action.
